analysis.one_liner: Lets federal K-12 and special education money follow students into private schools and homeschools.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 13 Republican sponsors and cosponsors and no Democratic support, was referred to the Education and Labor Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how federal elementary and secondary education money is distributed. Instead of flowing to school districts under the existing formulas, funds under Titles I through VI of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act would follow each child to whatever school they attend. Public schools would get a per-student share, while children in private schools or homeschools would get an equal amount deposited into an education savings account their family could spend on tuition, tutoring, books, technology, testing fees, and therapies for students with disabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who enroll their children in private schools or homeschool them would receive education savings account dollars for tuition, tutoring, curricula, technology, and educational therapies. Private schools would gain a new stream of federal tuition revenue, and education vendors and account administrators would gain a new market. Some families in districts with weak schools would gain an option to leave with funding in hand.

how_it_helps.text: Creates education savings accounts for children in private schools or homeschools, usable for private school tuition, tutoring, curriculum, online materials, testing fees, and educational therapies for students with disabilities.

Applies to funds under Titles I, III, IV, V, and VI of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and to Individuals with Disabilities Education Act funds, and explicitly lets the money follow students whether they are learning in person or remotely — written during the COVID-19 school closures of 2020.
Preserves eligibility for free and reduced-price school lunch for children who take the funds to private schools or homeschools.

analysis.who_pays: Public school districts and the students in them. Federal funds would be split into equal per-child amounts statewide regardless of where a child attends school, which removes the poverty weighting that directs Title I money to high-need schools. Districts would lose per-student funding as pupils left for private schools or homeschools while still carrying fixed costs like buildings, buses, and staff. Students remaining in public schools would attend schools with less federal money and no new accountability over how the diverted funds are spent.

drawbacks.text: The bill distributes federal K-12 funds in equal amounts per eligible child statewide, replacing the poverty-based targeting of Title I, so high-poverty schools would receive less federal money than under current law.

Public money would flow to private schools and homeschools through savings accounts while the bill expressly prohibits any federal or state control over non-public education providers, meaning the private schools receiving the funds would not be subject to the public accountability and service requirements that apply to public schools.

Federal K-12 funding is a small share of school budgets — roughly a few hundred dollars per child — far below most private school tuition, so the accounts would mostly supplement families who could already afford private schooling rather than open private school to low-income families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a family that has already chosen private school or homeschooling, the account is a straight gain: cash toward costs they are already bearing. For the roughly nine in ten children in public schools — and especially the low-income students Title I was written to serve — the trade runs the other way: money is spread away from need, drains out as classmates leave, and follows them to schools that the bill exempts from public oversight. On balance the bill's costs fall on the students with the fewest alternatives, while its benefits go largely to families who already have options.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Chip Roy introduced the bill on August 14, 2020, during the COVID-19 school closure period, with 10 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day, which was the only action it ever received.
The bill ended the Congress with no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no companion action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public school districts and the low-income students who depend on Title I's poverty-weighted funding are better off, because no federal K-12 or special education dollars were diverted to education savings accounts or private school tuition. Families who might have used the accounts gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Chip Roy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 14, 2020, proposing that federal K-12 and special education funds follow students to public, private, or home schools.

for.name: 12 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all listed cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

against.name: Chair Bobby Scott and the House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's only action was the referral itself.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans — 12 of the chamber's 197 House Republicans plus the sponsor — with no Democratic cosponsors, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would route federal education dollars to private schools as tuition through education savings accounts, while explicitly barring federal or state control over non-public education providers, so the schools would take public money without the accountability rules that bind public schools. Private school tuition typically exceeds the federal per-child amount, so the benefit flows mainly to families already able to afford private school.

Districts would lose per-student federal funds as students left for private schools or homeschools, and the equal per-child statewide split would strip the poverty weighting from Title I money, cutting federal aid to high-need schools. Public school interests and the low-income students they serve are on the same side here.

industries.industry: Education savings account administrators and financial firms
industries.note: The bill would create a new nationwide system of accounts holding federal education dollars, which requires an administrative and financial-services industry to operate. The firms' revenue comes from managing public education money diverted from schools.

industries.industry: Education vendors (tutoring, curriculum, online learning, testing)
industries.note: Allowable account uses include tutoring, curricula, online materials, diagnostic tools, and testing fees, opening a federally funded consumer market. Parents gain purchasing power, though the bill prohibits state or federal control over non-public providers, limiting quality oversight.
